title: Languages, logic and proof
subtitle: The vocabulary everything else is built on: strings, languages, and how to be sure a claim is true.

sections.title: Alphabets, strings and languages
sections.body: An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols, e.g. {0, 1}. A string is a finite sequence of them; ε is the empty string and Σ* the set of all strings. A language is any subset of Σ* — for example “all binary strings ending in 01”. The whole subject asks: how complicated a machine is needed to recognise a given language?

worked.why: Over Σ = {0, 1} how many strings have length exactly 3?
Two choices for each of three positions.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the empty string ε?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It has no symbol at all.

sections.title: Operations on languages
sections.body: From languages L and M: union L ∪ M, concatenation LM (a string of L followed by one of M) and the Kleene star L* (zero or more strings of L joined). If L = {a, b} then L* contains ε, a, b, aa, ab, … — every string over {a, b}.

choices.text: Yes — zero repetitions give the empty string.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Even if L itself does not contain ε.

sections.title: Propositional logic and inference
sections.body: Statements combine with ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies), ↔ (iff). Key rules: modus ponens (from P and P → Q, conclude Q), modus tollens (from ¬Q and P → Q, conclude ¬P). De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Predicate logic adds ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).

worked.why: Premises: “if it rains the match is cancelled” (R → C) and “the match was not cancelled” (¬C).

questions.prompt: From P → Q and Q, what can you conclude about P?

choices.text: Nothing — that is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

sections.title: Proof techniques
sections.body: Direct proof; contradiction (assume the opposite and derive an absurdity — e.g. √2 is irrational); induction (prove a base case and that n ⇒ n+1); the pigeonhole principle (n+1 pigeons in n holes: some hole has two — the engine behind the pumping lemma); diagonalisation (build an object that differs from the i-th item in the i-th place — proves the reals are uncountable and the halting problem undecidable).

worked.why: Base n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Step: assume it for n; adding n+1 gives n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2, the formula for n+1.

problems.prompt: How many strings of length ≤ 2 are there over {a, b}?
Let L = {ab}. List the first four strings of L*.

sections.title: The road ahead: the Chomsky hierarchy
sections.body: Four classes of language, each needing a stronger machine: regular (finite automaton) ⊂ context-free (pushdown automaton) ⊂ context-sensitive (linear-bounded automaton) ⊂ recursively enumerable (Turing machine). The rest of the course climbs this ladder.

questions.prompt: Which machine recognises exactly the context-free languages?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A finite control plus one stack.

figures.caption: Figure 1.5.1 — the Chomsky hierarchy
figures.note: Each class needs strictly more memory than the one inside it.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• A language is a set of strings over an alphabet; ∪, concatenation and * build new ones.
  • Proofs: direct, contradiction, induction, pigeonhole, diagonalisation.
